utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday. Good afternoon to everyone. Good afternoon, witness. The accused, the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and his team. And good afternoon to all the people assisting us. I think I told you you had 2 hours and 22 minutes left, Mr. Stringer. Without further adieu, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, good afternoon, Your Honours. Counsel and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday I was just about to take you to 1D 02994, which is in binder 3. It's the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm, sorry, 2994. During your direct testimony you referred us to Article 256 of this document which relates to the role of the municipality in respect of defence. It's on page 90 of the English version. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I had referred to the role on the local municipality in the constitution on in the role in defence and on undertaking all other responsibility that they had had at the local level including performance of the government functions at local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And I wanted to take you then to Article 273 of the same document, which is on page 95. This provides in part, I'll just read some of it: "In time of war in case of an immediate threat of war, a presidency of the Municipal Assembly shall be formed which shall decide questions within the competence of the Assembly. If it is impossible for the assembly to meet, composition of the presidency shall be established by law." And then it continues. Now, can we agree, Mr. Cvikl, that on the 8th of April, 1992 when the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued the declaration proclaiming the immediate threat of war, that that declaration then triggered this provision, Article 273?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, understand that the president issues such decree. And in that decree [indiscernible] also had said that the presidency shall be composed of the people that usually were in the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, which means elected representative. And then they also have said that they are extending the presidency with the then prime minister --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me that's a bit beyond the scope of my question. I'm simply asking, let me ask in general terms. Does the declaration of an imminent state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina then trigger the provisions found in 273?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, that's what was done at the level of the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and most likely the level of local community similar presidency had been established. It was a little bit more complicated because between this constitution of socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was adopted in 1974 and 1992 period, there were free elections, and I do not know whether free elections have resulted in anything on the change of the structure of the presidencies at the local level. But because of this, there should be some kind of executive authority in a smaller group than the Assembly of the local municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please turn to Exhibit 1D 00558, and that is in the same binder?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a decision issued by the Mostar municipality HVO. It's dated the 5th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it's one of the documents that's referred to in your report on page 82 when you are talking about financing. You don't need to -- you can go to it but I don't think it's necessary for you to go to your report about that. My question is this, it relates to something I asked you yesterday: When you were reviewing the decisions like this from the Mostar municipal HVO, did you consider whether the Mostar municipal HVO was the lawful entity under the law to be issuing decisions of this nature, rather than a war presidency of the municipality of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have he said already, between the enactment of constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina which must be somewhere around 1974 and 1992 there were free elections. How the free elections resulted in the change of the structure of the executive authorities at the local community, I do not know. But for certainly we know that there were free elections and the representative of different quote parties, that went on the elections in a particular local municipality. And out of that I understood in an area of Tuzla or in area of Jablanica or in area of Mostar, different either presidency or Defence Council or meetings of the president of the elected president of the local assembly with some other people were an active executive authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it then --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't know whether there was in existence at that time a war presidency of the municipality of Mostar because I don't know what has been happening in a particular. But clearly, the decision on the organisation the function in wartime finances in Mostar municipality is in its substance similar to the decisions established by similar executive authorities in other local municipality throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And that's without regard to whether such decisions were issued by something that were called itself a war presidency or whether it called itself a municipal HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Tuzla municipality it was issued by the president of the assembly and it was published in the Official Gazette of the municipality of Tuzla, so I do not know whether in this other case that was quote done exactly in accordance with what had been envisaged under the 1974 constitution where free elections had not been envisaged. The presidency of the local municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm -- I'm going --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers kindly slow down and not overlap for the sake of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to have to speak more slowly. And with respect, Mr. Cvikl, I think that you've answered the question sufficiently. We are not done yet you are going to have an opportunity to speak more to this issue. Can I direct your attention, please, to Exhibit 1D 00244. This dovetails with what you were just saying about the Tuzla municipality. 1D 00244. Now, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a decision issued by the president of the presidency of the Tuzla municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's dated the 4th of December, 1992. And I believe this is one of the documents actually you referred to in your testimony earlier as having been issued by Mr. Beslagic of the Tuzla municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I understood correctly, in fact, this is one of the documents that you discussed with him when you interviewed him in December of 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to understand the essence of the substance --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise I will just need to... I discussed this document with him as I discussed some other documents in order to understand what was the economic rationale for undertaking these measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And again, my only question here is in attempting to understand the rationale for undertaking these measure, you didn't distinguish or consider whether any given decision was issued by a war presidency, such as the case here, or a municipal HVO as is the case in the other document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been seeing different documents with a different titles on the top of the documents, and there were documents which were published in the Official Gazettes or they were are simply typed out on the different type machines in different local municipalities, and I was comparing the substance of those documents. And the substance of those documents were in my view, similar. And that is to undertake by the local municipality efforts to collect fiscal resources. So for them to be able to undertake what was the constitutional obligation and that is financing the defence. And this is what I understood was done at the local municipality in Mostar and that it was done in Tuzla, Zenica, Jablanica, et cetera, and these institutions undertaking these measures of different character. I can on Tuzla only say --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think that you've addressed the issue that I've asked you unless the Trial Chamber disagree, I am ready to move on. Now, Mr. Cvikl, I do want to ask you a few more questions about your meeting, your interview with Mr. Beslagic. As you indicated in your report, it took place on the 20th of December, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I have the impression that, if you recall, it must have been a fairly busy day for you. You had a number of these interviews on that same day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the morning in Zagreb and then was about 3 and a half 4 hour drive from Zagreb to Tuzla. Around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon I met with Mr. Beslagic and also Mr. Tanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. First -- well, earlier in the day then as I understand it you met with Mr. Neven Tomic and also according to your report you met where Mr. Mile Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So your interviews with both of those gentlemen took place in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both interviews with Mr. Tomic and Mr. Akmadzic took place in Zagreb in I believe Intercontinental Hotel. They lasted an hour, hour and a quarter each, and then early afternoon 1.30, 2.00 I drove to -- or, no -- around 2.00. 12.30 I drove to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you met with Mr. Beslagic and Mr. Tanovic jointly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a joint meeting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to direct you to Exhibit P 10763, which is in binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you repeat, 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P 10763. You can take that and you might want to put it on the table in front of you so that you can speak into the microphone. Mr. Cvikl, this is a witness statement that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Beslagic based on an interview that occurred on the 1st of September 2008, and it is subsequently earlier this month certified by the witness under Rule 92 bis. And in this statement -- do you have it there with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. I see it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this statement Mr. Beslagic discusses his meeting with you he is given an opportunity to comment on the various parts of your report that are attributed to him. And I've got some questions for you based on this. As you've indicated --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see this document first?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to take you to specific parts of it and we'll give you an opportunity to read --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is 17 pages long document and I would like to of course see what is the structure of the document and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if you will allow me I can explain the structure to you and we can walk through it together, we are not going to rush.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this document along with the following two documents, which is P 10764 and P 10765 were apparently statements taken by the Prosecution during the course of the break. Obviously which saw these for the first time yesterday. I understand the purpose of them, but however, if now the purpose is to impeach the witness through this statement, it would seem only appropriate to allow the witness the full opportunity to see this statement because this statement is -- was directly taken as a -- in response to the report prepared by Mr. Cvikl. Therefore I think in keeping with his request, the witness's request, he should be entitled to look at the entire statement before answering any questions. I think to just direct him to a particular passage is insufficient. And it shouldn't be up to me on redirect examination with the 13 minutes I have left to cover this material. And when we get to the third document, I will be objecting because in that document it would appear that the Prosecution is using the witness as a way of trying to contradict parts of not what was said but to use him as an expert witness as it were. And of course having no right of confrontation of the gentleman, we would object to that statement even being shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just briefly respond I think I can clarify one of the issues quickly that's been raised by counsel. The statements are to the extent that they are maybe tendered are tendered only for the purpose of impeachment. So there isn't any intention on the part of the Prosecution to submit any of these statements as evidence of anything for any other purpose. I know that is a live issue with the Trial Chamber at the present time but this is simply a matter for impeachment. What I propose is to continue with the cross-examination. If the Trial Chamber is uncomfortable with the way it unfolds or thinks the witness needs more time, I would suggest that we can consider that at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so Mr. Karnavas has sort of emphasized the fact that the witness needs time to look at what Selim Beslagic might have said, that's one thing, but the witness is very quit witted so he must have seen everything. Secondly, it seems that at the meeting of the 1st of December, 2008, Mr. Stringer was there because he interviewed Beslagic, so he must know everything very well about what might have been said. I can't see any interest or relevance in this type of interview whilst the proceedings are underway, but it is allowed by the case law of this Tribunal so it must be allowed here. But in civil law countries, this would be totally banned. Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, let me direct your attention on page 2 of the statement to paragraph 3. This begins with the meeting at the Hotel Tuzla with Mr. Beslagic and Mr. Tanovic. And in this part, Mr. Beslagic indicates that he actually suggested that Mr. Tanovic could come or should come because he had been more involved in financial issues for Tuzla municipality. Do you recall that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, I see this document for the first time. If I may first comment on the document is I appreciate the effort which was made and I can of course comment what was the fact, yes, we were together with Mr. Beslagic and Mr. Tanovic. Even in discussions which was a free flowing information where I was basically trying to understand what was the basis for some of the decisions made by the municipality of Tuzla where of course Mr. Beslagic confirms in the article, in the para 2, that he was the president of the quote war presidency Tuzla municipality, I'm saying this because I understood that he could also meet by himself as the war presidency that was needed. But then during the discussion, Mr. Tanovic was of course a man of more actual knowledge on the question which I was asking because he had been stated in my report, the head of basically finance department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he had of course -- he had more knowledge. I also did understood that Mr. Beslagic had some other private obligation that day, if I can recall that now, and he left after sometime. Was it one hour or one hour and quarter. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on paragraph 4, Mr. Beslagic says here that: "At the beginning of the interview, Mr. Cvikl informed me that according to Mr. Prlic, Herceg-Bosna did many of the same things that were done in Tuzla during the war in the financial or economic sphere." Is that true, Mr. Cvikl, did you inform Mr. Beslagic of Dr. Prlic's views on the similarities in activities between Herceg-Bosna and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how that he understood, but basically when I had been preparing a list of the witnesses which I wanted to see or at least the people which I wanted to see in order to ensure that I do understand correctly what had been sent, I had two type of situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, my question was not what he understood, it was a simple question. Did you make that statement to Mr. Beslagic informing him of what Mr. Prlic's views were? Did you make that statement that's attributed to you here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have said that I'm preparing -- may I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's a yes or no question or perhaps you don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been preparing a report, and I have mentioned to him that I'm preparing the report for the defence team of Mr. Prlic and it is based on the documents which are provided by Mr. Prlic Defence team, and I was referring to the documents. But I was not quoting that this is Mr. Prlic or Mr. Tomic or Mr. Akmadzic opinion. I have been just coming from Zagreb, and I will certainly mention that I am in a tour of the country, try to meet some of the people, and this is what was the purpose of my meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I mentioned this because some of the witnesses which I wanted to see when I contact them by the phone they were not willing to see me once I mentioned that I was working for the ICTY. That's why I perfectly made clear to those at the beginning what am I kind of doing. Some of them were not even wanted to meet me, like I would mention later one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Beslagic continuing where he says that he informed you that: "In Tuzla they at all times followed the laws and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not create new laws." He said: "I believe that all persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina were required to follow the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina whether or not it suited them at the time." Do you recall Mr. Beslagic saying that to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were discussing the basis of their issuing particular decisions, and we agreed that the decisions on the fiscal revenues were based on an overall decision on this decree by the law on the providing the needs to the socio-economic communities as identified and as requested by the war presidency -- by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And of course since we were coming from the same area, we both understood and know very well what is the -- what is the responsibility of the municipalities as far as the defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, paragraph 5, the first sentence, Mr. Beslagic states in fact that: "During the meeting no draft report and/or other documents were produced or discuss." So is it true, sir, that in fact you did not produce or discuss -- you did not produce with him any specific documents such as the one that we just looked at, the 1D 00244?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asking Mr. Beslagic on particular documents which they have produced. And I have been asking what does it mean for them, let's say, imposing the war tax on people that were actually trying to, you know, on particular war tax. And we were discussing what were the roles that the finance department was doing, and what they were doing in -- in the provision of the necessary funds for the refugees and people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So are you saying that --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had -- may I finish? I had my documents with me, I was making some notes of the documents because I was in discussing with them I was going through my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you share the documents him? Did you provide him an opportunity to look at them? He indicates that you did not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not a formal interview, the one that you undertook on the whenever it was. It was a discussion. I saw the documents. I wanted to discuss with the people what was the basis of the rationale for making these documents. I was not doing formal interviews. I was preparing a study and I needed to understand on the basis of the IMF and the World Bank study whether the events which were undertaken in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular local communities, were as depicted in these documents and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We know the scope of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, we know the scope of the report. You say now it's not a formal interview, but the fact is, Mr. Cvikl, that you have throughout your report attributed many statements to Mr. Beslagic naming him in interview foot notes, and you've done it for others as well. That would certainly indicate that this was something more than just an informal chat over coffee?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, you have to be, you have to understand how this report had been prepared. This report had been prepared on the basis of the documents. I could write this report without seeing these people. I wanted to be sure for myself what was actual developments. That's why I did this additional effort and went down there, but I did not approach in a formal manner the way you did. When I tied to approach to some of the people they were scared away. And so I had not, you know, called them upon formally. I have asked them would they be kind to see me so that we can discuss what we were discussing in 1994. I had met Mr. Beslagic for the first time in 1994, 1995. And at that time, you know, we got an opinion and what was happening, and we wrote this opinion, the World Bank team and the IMF in the report. Now I had their own documents. I tried to understood the basis what these documents were written. I have asked them whether there is a document which usually goes with the particular decree and that is a proposal for adoption of particular decision, and he said that something like that does not exist. So we have done on the basis of that have a discussion on the substance of those documents. But never as a formal interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am sorry to cut you off but I must. Therefore because it was not a formal interview, you did not share the actual documents with him that you've referred to or otherwise attributed to him; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, he has adopted these documents by himself as the head of the war presidency. I wanted to understand what was the reasoning for that. And the substance of these documents is known to him. So I see no need to present him his own documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. This is a document from 1992. You are saying that you see no need to present the document to him then when you met with him some 15 years later in 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Mr. Beslagic has been immediately at the beginning of the discussion informed me about his current discussions with authorities in Sarajevo, about what he was doing during the war. And during the war he is making an attempt by which he ensure that the thermal power-station in Tuzla was up and running. And for that very attempt, he, Mr. Beslagic himself, has order for the coal to be used. And he had explained to me that he had been sued by the federal authorities that he has been using this coal to heat the refugees. So he was to my knowledge quite familiar with what was happening in the 1992, 1996 period. He is currently a politician, he is a member of parliament, one of the parliaments, he is the federation parliament or republic of Bosnia parliament, and he had as politician exact knowledge on this substance. On details on finance the finance --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. I think I'll accept your answer. I think that's a sufficient answer to my last question. Let me ask you to turn to page 4 of this document. In paragraph 8 there is a reference and there's text that's linked to footnote 114 of your report, and you see the text from your report is set out right there in this statement beneath that in terms of format is the same text that's been translated. And then underneath that is the comment of Mr. Beslagic to the part of your report that is attributed to him, although we see here that this part of your report is actually attributed not only to Mr. Beslagic but to others as well. And this relates to the role of the municipal president which is something that you have written about and you've talked about. And what Mr. Beslagic says here is that he agrees that: "Under the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the local municipalities played an important role and had much greater responsibility after the declaration of a state of war in April 1992." Then he talks about: "The war presidency is the body that is envisioned under the constitution." I could take you down a few lines. He says: "However, I definitely did not say what is contained in the third sentence of this paragraph, starting with 'that was emphasized.'" Then he continues: "In Tuzla, the local representatives of the three nationalist parties, HDZ, SDA, and SDS did not hold positions of power in the Municipal Assembly and did not hold the position of president of the Municipal Assembly. I was a member of the reformist party." So would you agree with me, sir, that it is incorrect to attribute to Mr. Beslagic this part of your report which indicates that it was three political or the three national oriented parties that won the positions and served those roles in the Tuzla municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer that. To your question let me answer very detailed again. First of all the footnote 114 is a reference to the -- to my presentation what happened in local municipality post-free elections. And it confirms what I was saying before, that after first free elections depending on the results during those -- these first free elections there were, you know, the role of elected president of municipality was even stronger. Now, in here I'm mentioning three biggest political party. I apologise that I did not mention also the fourth political party which was Reformist Party or the so-called SDP, the former communist party or the former Markovic Party which was one of the party established at the level of the whole Yugoslavia trying prevent some of the events which were happening. And that's why I'm hear of course saying that this information was for me confirmed by the above-mentioned people, Mr. Pelivan, who was the prime minister of then the social -- sorry, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mr. Mile Akmadzic who replaced him as the prime minister . I was aware that Mr. Beslagic was one of the, you know, the political leaders that was in Tuzla able to prevent that either the Bosniaks led or Muslims led SDA or the Serbian SDA would prevail, right? But that's why I'm here saying that this interview with Mr. Pelivan, Mr. Akmadzic, and Mr. Beslagic has been of course confirming to me what am I saying in this paragraph after --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm just focusing on Tuzla. Mr. Beslagic indicates that this statement, the one he disputes, is not correct in respect of Tuzla. Isn't that true? In Tuzla it was not the chairman of the local branches of the HDZ, the SDA or the SDS that won the positions. That's not correct as applied to Tuzla, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article -- paragraph 54 of my report talks about all local municipalities, I have made a general statement. On all local municipalities on the basis of the results of the elections, this is not -- I did not making details on what was on each particular local assembly, and here I'm mentioning that the people that were explaining to me this were the one mentioned. And Mr. Beslagic was explaining to me that his role or his -- even today situation when he is a member of one of the not prevailing national based political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina was somehow different. But for the for the purposes of this Tribunal what I wanted to explain in the section 23.2, sectors contributing toward independent measures upon the war is that fact that after the free collections, local municipality elected officials being from one or the another party were stronger than before the first free elections and thus measures --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. You've said that and I'm sorry to cut you off. You have explained that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No but you are trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think anyone is disputing the increased power and role of the municipality in time of war. My question related to the political party composition in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but I understand that Mr. Beslagic in his comment saying that he is agreeing with my basic premise. He is disagreeing with the fact that he was not one of the three parties but he is actually the fourth party. But he is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that we agree.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So let me take you now --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was always the case in with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was not my argument. If the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think Mr. Cvikl, we've exhausted this point. I accept the distinction that you make, and if we could now move on to page 5?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would like of course for the honours present that if the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, my view of is that I don't frankly want to take more of my time to examine or discuss this footnote. If the Trial Chamber has any more questions on it I'm happy to defer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a footnote that I'm interested in, 710, paragraph 36. You have written that the local communities were indeed the only legal authority -- well, we will ask -- Mr. Stringer will ask the witness here what he thinks of that and will add something by adding also the districts. So for Mr. Beslagic, the local communities but also the districts that are the legal authorities. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am here in with the footnote 710 explaining the situation 1992, 1993 in areas under control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I understood that it was the most of the activity were undertaken by the local municipalities, I understand that there was the decree with the power of law on the establishment and work of districts established, but it was not fully put in place effectively. I have not seen any documents that would -- that had been presented to me where a particular decrees by particular districts in the area under control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were put in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in discussing with him, did you both agree on the fact that given the situation at the time and the siege of Sarajevo, that each on his part was doing the maximum via the local communities and the districts and that the areas under control of BiH, that's how it operated, and in the areas under control of the HVO it also operated in the same way? Did he agree with you on that or did he say I disagree because the HVO was illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had said -- he did not comment on this whether the HVO was legal or not. He had said to me that he was in contact with the HVO because for the goods to come into Tuzla, the goods has to come through the territory to which was at that time controlled under the, you know, HVO. So in that context he was in contact with them. And in that reference with your footnote, I also understood from his comment that as he mentioned previously, I'm now reading what you, Mr. Stringer has presented, page 16, as I mentioned previously, this must be comment which Mr. Beslagic, the ability of districts to actually implement changes was not great, however, districts as well as municipalities were the legal authorities. And I'm saying that in case of Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In case of Tuzla, I've seen most of the decisions or practically all decision which I have seen been decisions made by local municipality of Tuzla. But he had mentioned to me that when they had to apportion the strategic reserves in the strategic reserve warehouse which belong not to just one local community, they made an agreement at a regional district-wide level which means including other neighbouring municipalities. I have not seen, and I have been not presented on the -- for the area under the army of BiH controlled with any, maybe there were, districts decisions of meaningful effect. And that is exactly what he is also saying, that the ability of districts to actually implement changes was not great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually the next point of this statement that I wanted to take you to goes to this issue of the districts or the regionalization. It's on page 5. It's the text of your report that's linked to footnote 20 which again it should be statement to Mr. Beslagic, Tanovic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's paragraph 10 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Found on page 5. If you can look at --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No-no, but which footnote is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the text that's linked to that footnote relates to the need for -- well, it was just reading from your report: "It was realised that there were social administrative services that needed to be financed at a higher level than local community, regionalization, or the merging of local communities into a larger authorities within one budget took place..." and you continue. Then the last sentence of that says: "It must be noted that regionalization attempts were realised in several areas of BiH, in the Republika Srpska's local communities with Serbian majority population, in Herceg-Bosna's local communities with a Croat majority population, and in the regions around Tuzla, Velika Kladusa, Bihac, with the Muslim majority population." Now, Mr. Beslagic who does reject part of your assertion that is at least attributed to him, if you move down to his comment, he says that he does not dispute the first part of this citations, but he adds: "However, I never discussed the need for regionalization with Mr. Cvikl. The second part regarding regionalization attempts I do not accept this and I did not say this." Then he goes on to say: "The move toward regionalization in the Tuzla area came from the BH law on the establishment of districts." That's the law that you have referred to. He says he was appointed to reform the district for Tuzla area, however, he disagrees with the statement that the Tuzla district or region was established with a Muslim majority. He goes on to say: "I was not completely in favour of the decision establishing districts, but I followed it because it came from the presidency of RBiH and was the law. This part of the report refers to Republika Srpska and Herceg-Bosna districts in areas where Serb and Croat majorities lived. Unlike the decree on establishing districts, like the Tuzla district, the establishment of regions such as Republika Srpska or Herceg-Bosna were not in accordance with the law of the republic of BiH." So isn't it true, sir, that it's not correct to attribute to Mr. Beslagic these statements about regionalization and in fact you never discussed these issues with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not true. First of all, let me again explain to you, the discussion with Mr. Beslagic were on what was happening in the territory of Tuzla. And he is also mentioning the major problems which he had with the fact that refugees from the neighbouring local municipalities were coming into Tuzla. But he was taking care of those refugees. Then of course we were discussing what was there really an effected Tuzla district. And he said, there was not an effected Tuzla district. I understand that he nevertheless says here: "I was not completely in favour of the decision establishing district but I follow it because it came from the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was the law." I did understand that of course he was certainly the strongest person in town and that town of Tuzla is the centre of a much wider region where there are many local municipality. But legally speaking, he was the presidency of just of the municipality of Tuzla. What were his relation with whoever was appointed at the Tuzla district head, I do not know. But he was aware of the fact that there was a district, so he was aware that these districts are regionalization of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that's why I am in the footnote 120 where I'm discussing overall situation, I am of course quoting discussion with him, with his finance person, people from Jablanica, people from Mostar, and people from Livno. These were the people that were explaining to me that there was a problem if the local municipality were just left alone, so in that context, they were down the line, down the line, once they have seen that there are some positive effect of a well running regions, they were positive for that. Now, Mr. Beslagic was a person who was a mayor of as I have said Tuzla, but he has to take responsibility of the people that were not actually quote his people. So he was explaining to me what he was doing in ensuring that -- that very function, and so in that context he was for the people from the wider region the man that they had turned to him for the help. He was providing the central heating, he was providing food, he was ensuring what any local level -- local level responsible, not politician but responsible technocrat would do to take care of the people, that's what he was doing. And that's why we were discussing that, yes, it was difficult for him when he had only the resources of Tuzla. Even if you look down to the essence of the Tuzla decisions, the problems in Tuzla were not up to the point where they could have bringing goods from the north, south --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cvikl, I apologise for cutting you off. I think my question was intended to be more direct, which was simply this: I'll ask it this way: Mr. Beslagic say that the seconds part of that paragraph regarding regionalization attempts, he does not accept that and he did not say that to you. Do you agree with that or do you dispute his statement here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree because you are quoting the footnote 120, is a footnote which I'm commenting interviews with Beslagic, Bahrija Tanovic, Mirko Zelnika, Milenko Musa, Ile Krezo. This is the view which I got from all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, he is saying --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No-no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- sorry, may I intervene because perhaps there is a misunderstanding. I get the feeling that Mr. Beslagic had a different concept of "district" than the technical one. Because if you look at his comments, he speaks of Republika Srpska and Herceg-Bosna districts, and he -- I could imagine, and perhaps Mr. Cvikl, you can comment whether you would agree, that you use the term "district" with different meanings. Him thinking of Herceg-Bosna as a "district," you thinking of districts within the decree on the establishment of districts as districts which is of course much more work. Is it possible that there was such a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Districts, the way I defined them are the districts as I defined in the decree of the presidency of the districts. There are seven of them and the particular local municipality are assigned to them. And what am I saying? By the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let's not stray.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you convinced that your interlocutor, Mr. Beslagic, had the same concept when he speaks of districts and of regionalisation, because I think he had a different one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For his own district, Tuzla, yes, but he of course -- I don't know what was his view on Herceg-Bosna and Republika Srpska, I had not been discussing this with him because I -- I, you know, of course could only -- when we were discussing it is current legal framework of -- for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the one that he is happy with. He is not happy with it. Nobody is happy with it the way it is. So we are not discussing, we are not going into the much details, what does he thinks about the Herceg-Bosna and the Republika Srpska. But they were -- these two entities were region-wide authorities that tried to undertake what was envisaged in the presidency on districts to be undertaken by the district. Maybe not in the same group of communities, but the functions. There was -- there were a functions that were put to an institution between the central government on the local municipality, and he saw a need for such intermediate level to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think because of the time flying, what I want to do is move to the next exhibit, Mr. Cvikl, which should be right behind the one of we've just been looking at, it's 10764. We've discussed or the name of Mr. Bahrija Tanovic has come up and just a couple of question questions about Mr. Tanovic. You've already -- we've already discussed his role and the reason why he was at your meeting with Mr. Beslagic. What I want to do is direct you to the third page of this statement, and on -- well, you'll see at the top he makes reference to the meeting at the Hotel Tuzla, you were there with an assistant and an interpreter. Meeting lasted about an hour. I want to skip down to the second-to-last-paragraph there where he says that: "Before commenting on specific parts of the report that are attributed to me, I would like to clarify that I discussed with Mr. Cvikl the period of time prior to my departure for Zagreb in September 1992 or after, when I was appointed to the position of assistant to the president of the executive council for Tuzla municipality in April/May 1994. Because I was not present in Tuzla during September 1992 to mid-April 1993, and because I did not hold an official position in Tuzla municipality until April/May 1994, I am not in a position to comment on the various acts and decision of the Tuzla municipality or its war presidency during September 1992 until April/May 1994. "Any comments that I made for that period when I was in Zagreb and when I was not acting in an official capacity, I made as personal observations." And do you recall that, Mr. Cvikl, that in fact Mr. Tanovic was a representative of Tuzla who was based in Zagreb during that period of time trying to get humanitarian aid convoys arranged to come to Tuzla from outside?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had first established contact with Mr. Beslagic, and Mr. Beslagic suggest -- suggested that Mr. Tanovic shall be present at the meeting. Since Mr. Tanovic, I believe even today, holds the position of a director of a local branch of Tuzla Bank which is one of the, you know, more, I would say best -- one of better financial institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was very glad that he joined us to the meeting, and from the discussion with him whether he was -- we were not discussing what was his -- what was his official position. We were trying to understand what was happening in this very territory. Obviously, he had been connected with Mr. Beslagic and the action of the war presidency because that's what I assume under the fact that Mr. Beslagic actually suggested that Mr. Tanovic shall be in the meeting. And I was glad and from, you know, we are both commercial bankers, that's part of my career. We understood what we were talking when we were talking the financial decrees and the necessary actions to be undertaken to ensure that in Tuzla in 1992 and later in 1993 where the situation was much more difficult, efforts shall be made for those either humanitarian convoys or other goods and services to be brought into Tuzla region were done. So we were discussing as two economists, Mr. Beslagic I believe he is not an economist, what needed to be done in war period. So he had a very good knowledge of that war period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he understand that the things he was saying to you in this informal meeting would be placed in your report as footnotes and presented to the Judges in this case? At this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said before, let me now explain this to you and to the Judges. In preparing this report, I studied documents. I did not want to finish the report without reconnect myself by going down to Tuzla, Sarajevo, and Mostar where I was last time in 2001, 2002 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cvikl, you've explained to us and we understand fully your motivations and your wishes to go speak to people on the ground in the region. My question was a different one. It was whether Mr. Tanovic understood or knew that the things he was saying to you in this meeting would find themselves and find their way into this report, footnoted, attributed to him by name in footnotes, and then presented to the Judges in this trial as evidence? Did he know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He understood that I am preparing a report. He was -- I was not approached by him in the way because that was never the purpose of my preparing the report. I was not running an investigation. I did not go there to ask for the witness statement. I was making discussions in a free flow with them to -- for my understanding of the situation on the basis of the documents which I have reviewed, and they had a very good knowledge of. And the way I approached this was because that was the only way how I could have actual conversation with them. Because as I have said, there were a couple of peoples that I wanted to see but they did not want to meet anyone when I mentioned that this is linked with the Defence -- sorry, with the ICTY Tribunal. On the other side, there were documents and I needed to understand those documents. And Mr. Tanovic and Mr. Beslagic were in a free will presenting me the facts which of course are also -- were confirming to me what the documents were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that you withheld information or you misled these people into meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not misled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you didn't tell them that in fact they would find their way -- their names would be footnoted in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may -- excuse me, Mr. Cvikl. I object to this line of questioning. Now, he is trying to insinuate that Mr. Cvikl lied to these people. He had represented himself to be there, to write a report, or to gather information because he was writing a report on behalf of the Prlic Defence team. That was rather transparent. Now, whether he indeed -- they obviously knew that he was writing a report, they could see him taking notes. Whether he represented to them that they were going to find themselves in, that's another story, but to insinuate -- to insinuate -- let me -- if I -- may I be allowed to make my record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, what are you doing? You are [Microphone not activated] if he answer then the witness [Microphone not activated] Chamber what the witness did and what the witness could expect it from the people with whom he spoke because that's a question Mr. Stringer asked the witness. Now you are giving the answer and you are not suppose today do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand what I'm supposed to do and not to do. I think I've done this quite a bit, and I think I understand the rules, Judge Trechsel. I certainly don't need a lecture from the Bench on this issue. What I should reminds the Trial Chamber, however, is if the Trial Chamber looks at the previous answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- he has given -- I'm not saying anything that hasn't been in the record. It's all in the record. And I would expect from the bench to say, Asked and answered. Move on Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Judges are not here to lecture you, but they are here to make sure that the examination takes place in proper conditions. Witness, it is true that in a footnote in your report you said interview with such and such a person, for instance with Mr. Beslagic. When you gave this report to the counsel, did he say or did he ask you this, Well, you put it down in your report, but do you know that in so doing the Prosecutor who's got enormous means at his disposal can go to see those people and to ascertain that those people did indeed say that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's why my response to Mr. Stringer question. I have not misled the people. The people that were not willing to discuss with me, I did not interview them. All the people which I interviewed were the people that I have informed of what am I doing during my visit. And in that context I was acting in the same manner as we were acting 1994, 1996 period when we, the World Bank team and the IMF team, have discussion with the people and presenting that this is what we are going to put in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. But whilst I was listening to you earlier on, I was under the impression that this Tribunal is not well seen in the area because as soon as its name is mentioned there's a kind of hostility that appears. When you talk to these people, did you tell them that you were going to quote them in your report and that possibly the OTP might ask them to confirm what they said to you? Did you say that officially to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never -- when I was writing an economic report, I was not doing an investigation. I was righting an economic report and I wanted to -- I could write this report without having interviews. But then me myself would need other means, other means to how to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, but we are not going to dwell on it because I know that you are a very busy man. But when you met with these individuals who are well known people and you had this informal interview as part of your study, find of the report, the problem is that the report was handed in a court of law and everything is examined minutiously, especially by the Prosecution since you are a Defence witness. So in the future if you are asked to write a report it's better to tell the person you are speaking to that you are writing a report for the Defence, can I quote you. And the person can then say "yes" or "no" and this kind of problem can be avoided. But that's for the future. Now it's too late. Mr. Stringer, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly what I did. I have told to the people that I am writing a report and that some of their -- or views, some of their opinions would be part of my report. But of course I did not go to see the people that would be only confirming what I intended to say. I wanted to have different views. That's why I went to see different people. I mean, that is the whole essence. And the discussion with Mr. Beslagic and the discussion with Mr. Tanovic were for me fruitful for my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, one last question on the issue of districts. I'm looking at page 105 of your report. You can set aside the witness statement. We are going to move on. Page 105 of your report, it relates to what's been discussed the last couple of minutes. On page 5 -- sorry, paragraph 5. "Analysis of the development in Croat majority areas confirms that, not surprisingly, later in the war period especially, in the second and third phase, economic development in areas with a Croat majority was very much in line with the authority vested in districts by the presidency decree with power of law on the establishment of work districts." And I wanted to try to get a clarification of that. Are you suggesting that the regionalization in Herceg-Bosna was pursuant to the decree law that is a -- in a legal sense, if you will, or when you say "very much in line with," are you saying that it was similar or consistent with the provisions that are found in the decree law? Do you see the distinction there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, could you rephrase it please, and please can you use another term than "pursuant."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Here you are saying that in the Croat majority area, which I understand we can refer to generically as Herceg-Bosna, that the economic development was very much in line with the authority vested in the districts by the Bosnia-Herzegovina decree, right. And there are two ways I think somebody could interpret that. On the one hand somebody could say, Oh, yeah, there was a decree issued by the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the basis of that decree, we followed that decree and we accepted it and we formed a district which -- in Herceg-Bosna which is very much in line, right, with the authorities granted by the decree. That's one interpretation. Another possible interpretation, I would suggest, is that what they did in Herceg-Bosna was consistent with in many ways, the provisions of the decree, but they did so independently. They did it on their own and not as a result of the decree itself. So my question is, when you say it was very much in line with the authority, are you saying it was -- they accepted the authority and followed suit, or did act in a similar way but independently?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here my paragraph talks about that the analysis confirms that the developments, economic development, in areas was very much in line with the authority vested, which means that the presidency decree with the power of law in the inception work of district define what particular departments, line ministries of districts. Should there be one supposed and allowed to do? And these are usually - and that was the case in the case of district three - authorities of the central government. So the presidency has decided that the authorities of the central government is transferred down to the region. At the same time, once under the base of the Bosnian constitutions, local communities started to act, and they've acted on the basis of the of the decree of the so-called necessary financing of the socio-economic needs, they have the basis to take and to adopt fiscal regulation, et cetera. But there was then a problem, that in local municipalities of a different economic welfare, the situation was different, so at the local level there was a need being to recognised that there shall be a region-wide measures undertaken. So whatever was I was seeing in the second phase of the HVO were actually trying to make measures that were initially undertaken at the level of the local municipality to be varied for the wider region, and as I'm saying in the last paragraph -- last sentence in that paragraph, they have not undertaken all the activities that was vested down by the presidency decree of August 1992. And I assumed that there were two simultaneous activities: The presidency recognizing that they cannot control the country and that they would not want to have 50 or 70 small economic areas, and at the level the local communities there was a need to recognise that for the economy of scale, in order to undertake measures that would not be good just for one local community, there has to be some of those measures undertaken. And I am mentioning two very cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the road to salvation and starting of the school year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Are you aware whether the leadership of Herceg-Bosna expressly repudiated and rejected implementation of the decree on establishment of work districts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. The next topic goes to the issue of financing of the military, and specifically, I want to focus on Herceg-Bosna and the financing of the HVO. And if I can take you again to your report, Mr. Cvikl, pages 72 and 73, there's some passages there that relate to this. I'm looking on page 72 at section 4.3.1, Croat local community measures aimed at financing defence. And here you first refer to the Mostar municipality and you refer to some legislation; for example, the establishment of a separate account that provided a framework to finance defence activities in Mostar. And then turning the page you have a section there on measures taken in Livno, again your citing some decisions taken by the Livno HVO authorities with a view toward financing the activities of the Bruno Busic HVO regiment. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, and let me ask this way: Correct me if I'm wrong, in the earlier, perhaps the phase 1 period, as I understand from your testimony, the municipalities were more active in all ways or perhaps had more authority and were more active in financing activities, but as time went on, just moving into 1993, it was the HVO that - from a more central point of view - was funding defence activities. Is that a correct understanding, or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not because it depends very much what was the situation in particular local municipality, and we discussed this with one of the -- some of the documents which was yesterday presented where one of the other Defence counsels, we were actually discussing this Bruno Busic HVO regiment. But it was obviously that the funds that were supposed to be given to Livno were not sufficient, so they went and undertake some additional measures. The Livno municipality and the Mostar municipality measures, and, yeah, are an examples what type of measures were aimed at financing defence. The one that I have been collected. There must have been some others. We have seen some of those, we could quote them here, you know, what we were doing in Travnik, what they were doing in Zenica. This is Travnik at the time of the -- of being in the first part. So these are the type of the measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT

utterances.text: Yes. Question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Articles 170 on the decree of armed forces provides that: "Funding of the armed forces of the HZ HB shall be carried out according to the budget of the defence department, adopted by member municipalities of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, Article 170 had been issued and is a part of a decree which was issued in October of, I believe, 1992. Right? From referring to the page 139 where I'm explaining this what is happening, if I'm not correct, this is 742, here we are discussing the problems. This is the so-called section on continuation of independent economic measures by local communities in Croat majority area. So despite the fact that there were attempts in the phase 2, under the phase 2 was already there, and there were institutions established, still as we have seen from some of the cases - one of them which you also mentioned - there were of course -- there were independent measures undertaken. And decision of -- just a second, that was the Prozor, that is the Prozor that is February 18, 1993, what was the actual situation -- sorry, we have to be very careful. utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question from another standpoint, from another angle, and I think it is a capital question. This Article 170, while we see that in during the events the administration could come up very quickly with a text of close to 170 articles, you would think that all the beaurocrats were spending their time writing text of the kind, but as to Article 170, it says very officially, and that the budget of the defence department must be adopted by the municipalities. Very well. But in a democratic system, the budget of the Defence ministry is adopted by the parliament, but for a few countries where the head of state can commit money for military purposes, but as a rule, the budget is adopted democratically by the members of parliament. But here we have adoption by the communities, as part of the war effort. I have Mr. Prlic, I have Mr. Stojic, and the members of the government which I put in relation to the municipalities. What margin for manoeuvre did they have if indeed it was the municipalities that had some power over their revenues, and secondly, would approve or not approve the budget. In such a context what can a government such as the HVO government do? You are an economist, you have budgetary knowledge and you've held high-ranking political functions, can you as such tell me what is the real scope of Article 170 in relation to the ministry of defence, to Mr. Prlic, to Mr. Boban, tell me if this is too complicated a question. You just say you don't want to answer and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think with you have, of course, pointed to the gist of the problem. And that is that when some of this legislation was written, especially the one on the decree on the arms forces the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I'm not aware and it doesn't look like that they have taken into account, you know, the over executive authority already been established. On the other side we have seen some local municipalities undertaking a very similar measures to adopt decree on how in the wartime over-financing shall be organised, that there should be revenues and there should be expenditures. And so if the first phase would continue throughout 1991, 1994 period, we would most likely have a situation where local municipality would be, you know, sitting on their own money, and region-wide measures would not be undertaken and no region-wide even defence activity could be -- could be assured. So I do understood or I understand that whatever it was done in the second phase and in third phase was an uphill battle, uphill battle by the executive authorities being established there to somehow undertake measures necessary at the level of the region. Okay, I have said already as envisaged under the presidency decree of the districts, that would ensure that, you know, this local municipalities would be much more economically connected in all matters, including the defence, including the provision of other social and state services. And that was ultimate economic role of these executive authority. And I would, of course, say that they were -- they were -- it was positive that they were undertaking this, because if they would not have been undertaking this, you would have 50 or 70 small economies all around Bosnia-Herzegovina which ultimately -- 50, 70 small armies depending on who would be able to be better equipped. So Article 170 provides not, it could imply that this budget of the defence department would be once upon a time a part of the overall budget, and I have appreciated that in the second and the third phase such things have happened, but, you know, the way initially was this design, it's difficult to say what were, you know, views of the people writing it. Now, just my last comments on, you know, why 170 articles, you know, lost -- this legislation had been, you know, put in place and at that time, you know, this was, you know, you know, people have this -- had the skills, you know, local municipalities and people have the skills preparing such legislation. That was not surprise to me. I've seen that even in other local municipalities.
