I'm putting to him in fact that there is a very different, very substantial level of funding that's coming from the Croatian ministry of defence which, with respect, is not an issue that he has addressed or accounted for in his report. I'm ready now to go to the budget and to talk about the budget of the Herceg-Bosna for 1993 and how this relates to the Herceg-Bosna budget for 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, if I could, Mr. Cvikl, ask you to turn to page 157 of your report, and we can put that up on the screens. We've got it in Sanction because it might facilitate all of our work in looking at this particular page. Sorry, you are seeing it on the screen. Thank you. This is, Mr. Cvikl, from your report, but can we agree that these figures -- actually, you took these directly from that HVO report on work for 1993 that had the work of the different departments, and this came from the Ministry of Finance or the department of finance section and is their budget.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed that yesterday, this is the source, this is the economic department, the reports by different departments I guess collected by the economics department and those are the revenues which obviously went through the budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And for the record, Mr. President, the exhibit on that is P 09551. That's that HVO work report. Okay. A couple of questions on some of these numbers, Mr. Cvikl, if I could direct your attention first of all to item 1.6 which relates to customs. And of course we are on the revenue side of the budget now, the money coming in to the HZ HB budget during 1993, item 1.6 relating to customs. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I understand correctly, this figure is represents the amount of money that would have been raised by the Herceg-Bosna authorities in collecting duties and customs, taxes, if you will, as part of obviously the customs function that's being carried out by Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be most likely the budget prepared under the cash principle, which means that those budget, those customs, and those transfer which were made in cash and were going via budget would be, if normal practices were respected, presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And would you agree with me, sir, that that figure accounts for nearly one-quarter of the budget revenues of Herceg-Bosna for 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As presented in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And under the assumption that all revenues are cash revenues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next item I wanted to ask you about is item number 3, which is toward the bottom, which relates to revenues from credits, i.e., financing of deficit. Now, in your testimony earlier, you indicated that you thought that these funds represented commercial borrowing by the Herceg-Bosna authorities, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I assist you to find something?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: P 09 -- yeah, just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While you are finding that, I'll just read you an excerpt of your testimony from earlier this week, page 35303. You were asked about this and you said --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the report, the Croatian version, it says, number 3 revenues from credits. I added that this in a normal budget presentation, these revenues of credits would be financing the deficit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in your testimony earlier you said that: "I understand these are the revenues from credit mainly provided by commercial banks because we have not seen and I have not seen any central bank being created on the territory of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which means that also these revenues from credits have been backed by some savings in commercial banks. And I guess that that was at the time mainly so-called Hrvatska banka, Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my question, sir, is do you know - and I'll put it to in fact - you don't know whether in fact all of these loans from Croatia that we've seen are reflected on this item, line item 3, in the budget of Herceg-Bosna, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, when I say that these are the revenues from the credits and that means that they are not printed monies, my statement goes in connection that there were no central bank authority at the level of Herceg-Bosna, which means that the revenues of credits were replaced by real savings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's -- and the reason why I, of course, emphasized this is because in 1993 the lower inflation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in this very territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was lower than in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am sorry, I'm going to have to cut you off here. Do you know whether the loans represented in the documentation we've been looking at is reflected anywhere in the budget of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have taken as a basis the report of the so-called Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. And isn't it true that that report does not indicate that the Republic of Croatia was providing this level of loan funding to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it true that --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the transcript, please, on my left screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll re-ask the question. Isn't it true, Mr. Cvikl, that the work report does not indicate or reveal that in fact Republic of Croatia is providing these loans. It's not in the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that -- my purpose of analysis was not comparing whether in a particular revenues of the budget of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was everything what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not doing the external audit of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and financing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been presenting --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No-no, we understand what you have been presenting --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been presenting that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, the answer is no, I think, and that's it, okay. You continue, you continue not to follow the rules and you talk and talk instead of simply giving answers. I'm sorry, this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, you do not have to comment. The rules are here we make the rules you have to comply with them. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer "no" to a question which is not correctly put.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: How is the question of whether these loans figure in the papers not correctly put? You can say they do, they don't, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody had made analogies and so that's what in my answer is not no, my answer is I don't recall, or I don't know because I did not make this analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's okay. That's okay. You can answer like this, perfect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how I answered, I answered that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No-no, you started speaking -- Mr. Stringer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Item number 4, grants and other revenues, and that accounts for about a quarter of the budget. Do you know what the grants and other revenues consist of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In normal circumstances the grants and other revenues would consist of the official grants by other countries or other entities that are not from the local, and they usually would present the nominal value if they respect the cash flow principle. If they do not respect the cash flow principle which was usually the case, the grants and revenues in the amount of the old -- what we have seen would not be presented here. Nobody, neither myself had made an analyses what is behind these line items at 3 or 4, so one cannot actually said what level of the grants coming to Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was really presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that one quarter of the revenues --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No-no --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is covered by the grants. That's the essence of this table. We have a normal structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. What are the source of grants and other revenues? Do you know? Where do those come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well according to the legislation being in place and according to the chart of accounts, the grants and other revenues have to come from other countries that, the is rule of the games in the chart of accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. Now I'm asking about this specific number, 57.495.000.000 Croatian dinars, what's the source of those Croatian dinars, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I also don't know what were the sources and what kind of customs proceeds were coming in. This is the report which only shows that in the year 1993 they were collecting more revenues than in the year 1992. In the year 1994 they collected even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you, I'm going to move on to the next item. I'm going to ask you some questions about your meeting with Mr. Backovic. Now, you can turn in the second binder to 10765 which is the statement that Mr. Backovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor said 50 billion. Just to avoid any misunderstandings between the American and European markings, it's 50 -- in English it's billion, in Europe it's -- the difference is three zeros.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You have the statement that was provided by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, your mike is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have 10765, the statement by Mr. Backovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As I understand you met him for about an hour at the Holiday Inn hotel in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And although you've indicated in your report correctly that Mr. Backovic is a former vice-governor of the Central Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you agree with me, Mr. Cvikl, that in fact he was not a vice-governor of the central bank during the time-period largely covered by your report 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just two sentences first. On those grants whose institutions are described in the economics report of the Bosnian authorities, and I mention UNICEF, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No-no, no, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just saying to you because you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No-no, no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who they are. It said that in the reports there are the names. Well, Mr. Backovic, I met Mr. Backovic for the first time in 1994, 1995 when he was vice-governor of at that time National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. And we'll get to that, I assure you my question was more limited; that is, he was not vice-governor of the central bank at the time of 1992 and 1993. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him -- when I met him for the first time, he was vice-governor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. But --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't know what he was doing in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was -- I know him as a vice-governor of National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, and is he one of the people who you didn't -- you didn't share with him the fact that you were preparing an expert report that would cite him because you were concerned that if you did so he might not agree to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not true. The people who are not agreeing once I present them over the phone, my attempt -- I did not even have discussions with them. I had a discussion with him where I presented to him that I am in Sarajevo again after couple of years, and I'm preparing a report where I would try to understand what was happening on the monetary area. And he had basically -- he knew of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And once you prepared your report or your draft of your report, I take it even though you were citing him as vice-governor, you never gave him an opportunity to review the statements that you were attributing to him; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to repeat here what I have already said. I have not made formal interviews, and I have been discussing with Mr. Backovic in the same manner as with Mr. Enis Gotovusa [phoen], but I'm having with him a discussion because I was asked to prepare a report on what was happening. And on the basis of the IMF and the World Bank report where he had been cooperating with us very extensively, I wanted with him to reiterate some of the findings in the 1994, 1996 period when I was in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I wanted to here from talking to him and talking to another person, I wanted to find out what was happening in the central bank at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm looking at page 3 of his statement at the top where he says that: "It's important to keep in mind during 1992 and most of 1993, I was working as deputy general manager with a commercial bank, Kreditna banka Sarajevo, not with the National Bank of RBiH. I informed Mr. Cvikl that I was not the person in the best position to give information about the economic and financial actions of the government authorities during 1992 and most of 1993." And then he continues on to name some people that he suggested you should go to talk to who would be in a better position. Do you recall that, sir? Do you recall Mr. Backovic telling you that there were others who were better positioned to answer your questions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that and I tried to meet Mr. Stijepo Andric who was governor of the National Bank of Herzegovina in Slovenia but I was not successful in meeting him. And I was trying to also make an effort to establish contact with Mr. Krezo. He, as I can see he also was suggesting that I meet Mr. Mikovic [phoen] before on many occasions, and he is also suggesting that I should be meeting Mr. Krezo and Mr. -- because the book was revised by academic professor Dr. Ivo Perisin. I know of Ivo Perisin. He was my colleague when I was at the National Bank of Yugoslavia. However, since Mr. Perisin was a regular member of the Croatian Academy of Science and Art, I did not want to have discussions on the monetary issue just with the Croats. I wanted to hear from a non-Croat such an opinion. And certainly I did not want to hear it only from people that, like Mr. Andric, who left as a governor afterwards. But that's why I intended to meet Mr. Backovic. And I understand also on page 2 that he said that it was in understood that the war which undertaking is linked with the preparation of the Prlic Defence. So he was aware of that, he is confirming what you were implying before that hes not aware of. I'm just reading what he has said to you or to your inquiry. So he was aware that we are discussing the issues linked with my work on the preparation of the -- of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the defence. And I had with me the IMF report and I had with me the World Bank report, and we went through some of these already in these two report identified major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. And just continuing from the passage on page 2 that you've just referred to, it is true, sir, isn't it that Mr. Cvikl, that you did not inform Mr. Backovic that his opinions given to you would be cited in your report and then submitted to judges at this Tribunal; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would repeat again what I have said. I did not went to see Mr. Backovic for get his - how shall I say? - confirmation of my belief. I wanted to hear his opinion. And I presented his opinion in the same manner as I presented the opinion of other people, and as I presented the views expressed in the reports of the IMF and the World Bank to which Mr. Backovic was main counterpart on the Bosnian side. So he was -- what he was saying to me in 9th 2007 is the same thing which he was saying to me in 1994, 1996 period, and that is that the monetary authorities were not up and running.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid all the time on this, the fact that you've cited names of people who subsequently will more or less say the opposite, why did you not envisage the following procedure: When your report was completed, you could ask your secretary to have a standard correspondence to these certain individuals saying, Dear sirs, I'm addressing here with a copy of a report that I will be presenting to the ICTY pertaining to a request put forward by the Prlic Defence. Your name appearing on page X, Y, or Z, I would be grateful if you could let me know as soon as possible whether you have any observations to make, it being stated of course that I have to convey to my counsel this draft by a specific date. And therein you just quietly wait for a response. Did that idea not occur to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did the same work in the same manner as we do it as -- as we have done it in the World Bank. We in the beginning of the 1996 report, we make acknowledgments, but we are not and we have never been requesting from the people whether the analysis that the way we make it is -- is the one which, quote, will then confirm, because this is not -- this is not analysis and this is not a report, I would be make it -- simply doing what the Prosecutor was doing, which is taking the witness statement. I was not asked to do -- to investigate -- to investigate. I wanted for my understanding to see whether the situation described in the two reports, and additionally confirmed, additionally confirmed by many documents which were -- which were presented to me are in the manner that we have seen them in the 1994. And here on the evolution of monetary policy institutions between 1992, 1995, that is being already written in 1996, and I cited extensively throughout this report - this is my first footnote - I say, I am basing my analysis on the two most important documents. When I go into the details, when I go into details, I present additional information which were at that time not valid. And that is mostly to do with what is happening on the level of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but let me just take the footnote, say at page 398 where you say in paragraph 41 that: "In the education sector the individual and local communities were the only ones capable of meeting the needs of the elementary schools." And you cite three individuals who would seem to attest to that, Milenko Musa and Ile Krezo -- not three but two individuals. Let's assume for a second that they disagree, they disagree. They believe that there were other fundings. You see where the problem is? In support of your claims you cite people, but if people disagree -- do you see that's the risk, that's the danger. We are not in the World Bank where you can say just anything. You are before a judicial institution where everything that is written will be screened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But on this very footnote which you are mentioning, we were discussing with Mr. Milenko Musa and with Mr. Krezo what has been written in the HVO report. In the HVO report has been written that the local communities were starting to provide assistance. I was trying to confirm from them whether what has been written in the HVO report is correct in the same manner as I was with Mr. Backovic discussing, you know, when actually monetary authorities of National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina took control of that area. And he had confirmed to me as I see have seen it still in 1995 that they did not have this control. 1992, 1993, 1994, even up to 1995 they did not have this control. That was the whole essence of my finding because there was a lack of control by the monetary authorities somebody else step into it. And that's who was somebody else were local communities all over the place. And I wanted to -- I wanted to hear from them whether that was correct and that's what Mr. Backovic was confirming to me. I have seen this by myself. This is what we -- we, the IMF and the World Bank wrote in 1996. There were different monetary arrangement in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Getting back to the statement of Mr. Backovic, though, looking back at page 3 now, the second-to-last paragraph begins with the word "third," and I just want to move up a few lines. He is talking about your meeting at the Holiday Inn which lasted about an hour and he says: "During our conversation we spoke in general terms about economic and financial issues that he discusses in his report ..." that's your report, "... without discussing any details. Third, I wish to state that I have seen Mr. Cvikl's report and all of the footnotes and text that refer to me. With regard to all of those footnotes I state that I do not accept the text that is attributed to me because such detailed comments could not correspond with a short informal meeting such as I had with Mr. Cvikl in December of 2007." Now, isn't that true, sir? You had coffee, you had a chat at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo, you have discussed matters which have taken us weeks to cover with other witnesses, such as Mr. Tomic, and the fact is the level of complexity of these issues is such that they can't be discussed in detail -- at this level of detail --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- on the basis of a short conversation over coffee?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Backovic was a vice-governor National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was the main counterpart to two reports, the IMF report and the World Bank report, and we were discussing the substance of these two reports. He was vice-governor, he is professor, if I ask him, What was the money demand for Bosnian dinar, and he respond to me, The money demand was very weak, was very low, that is for me as an economist an explanation that nobody seriously, as has been presented on the place, really took Bosnian dinar as a convertible and as a respectful currency. This was, Mr. Stringer, actually the reasoning why in the Dayton agreement we have had a new central bank to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, since you brought up the issue of currency, let's then move to page 4 of Mr. Backovic's statement. I'm going to refer you to paragraph 6 there of the statement, which refers to footnote 80 of your report and the text that's linked to that. And there, under that text, you indicate in your report that: First republican authorities delayed issuance of the new currency despite the fact that the Yugoslav dinar had cease today exist as legal tender once Bosnia-Herzegovina was established as a sovereign state. And then you go on about the Yugoslav dinar being used in BiH. Now, this is what Mr. Backovic says, he says: "He says it's true the situation was complicated, however, the republican authorities did not intentionally delay. Delay was the result of a complicated situation which made more difficult the technical realisation of decisions; for example, there was significant time difference between the referendum vote for BiH independence and the official international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina." He goes on to talk about technical issues on the printing of money and the stamp that was used on Yugoslav dinar bills. Now, isn't it true that even in Slovenia there was a three-month delay in the issuance of any form of Slovenian currency three months after Slovenia declared its independence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, first of all the 3 month delay in Slovenian was linked with the Brioni agreement where we have, instead of issuing the currency on the 25th of June, have agreed that we will do it 3 months later at the time when the Yugoslav Army left the country. On the statement of Mr. Backovic, I think we have a common position. I have said republican authorities delayed the issuance. I did not say that they intentionally have done that. I explained in my testimony and in the report. If this was because of the military activities, because of inability of the central government, I was even reading that once dinar were printed, UNPROFOR did not want it to -- to bring it to Sarajevo. So I never said that the authorities intentionally have not done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was the situation. It was a military situation, and you should not be comparing it with Slovenia, because in Slovenia on the purpose we upon the signing of the Brioni agreement agreed we would do this with a three month delay which was on 8th of October and then it was done overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, on this intentional delay this raises another issue, a more general one that I have been meaning to ask you. Because if one reads your report, you very steadily refer throughout your report to the fact that the central government didn't do things, failed to do things, or was unable to do things. And one could read that as criticism, that the central government through incompetence or through lack of intention or through some malfeasance failed to do things that it could have done. Now, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My position is that the central government could do two things on the money issues. They could -- they could issue new currency, but what is even more important they could -- they could limit themselves on the financing of the budget. Because if they would do the other, that means that they would have a more economically stable situation. And I'm not saying whether it was right or wrong. I'm describing that because they have decided to print cash needed, 98 percent of the war budget was financed by printing, they created a hyperinflation environment in which, in which people did not trust BH dinar and that's why para-currency was put in place. This is my analysis. I'm not blaming anyone for what was happening. I'm only say that the BH dinar, because there was oversupply of the BH dinar, not being covered created hyperinflation environment in which usually para-currency took place. In the case of Slovenia we issued new currency but we limit ourselves to not print it above the supply needed and thus we had reduced inflation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the time this three-month period in which -- between Slovenian independence and the actual introduction of the new currency, Slovenia fortunately was not occupied nearly at all, and it certainly wasn't occupied -- two-thirds of its territory is not occupied by Serb forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You again implying that I'm criticizing the central government authorities. I'm not criticizing them. I'm only saying that the situation was such that they decided to print funds, even as Mr. Backovic says, they started marking Yugoslav dinars in a special way, with a stamp, and this basically represented the legal method of payment in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were doing such some measures which all created lack of trust in the central government authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you would turn to page 7 of Mr. Backovic's statement. Paragraph 11. This relates to an issue that you have mentioned also just in the last few minutes, that is the functioning of the banking system. In your report it's indicated here, you say that the ongoing military actions - this is page 44 of your report - ongoing military actions also caused the banking system to stop functioning. And that's supported in your footnote 142 by your interviews with Mr. Tomic and Mr. Backovic. But isn't it true, sir, as Mr. Backovic indicates here that it's exaggerated to say that the banking system stopped functioning. It's true the same system functioned under very difficult conditions. He indicates to his knowledge no commercial banks on the territory under control of the legal authorities of Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina fully stopped working during the aggression. However, you cannot expect banks to operate in full capacity during the war, the national bank never stopped working. So isn't that true, sir, isn't it an exaggeration to suggest that the banking system was 100 percent not functioning?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the banks the most important is the trust. And once with the war people could not go to the bank and withdraw that deposits, the trust into the banking system is gone. And that's why, yes, there were premises more or less empty. We have still see these premises empty in 1995, 1996 when he came there. Industrial production dropped 91 percent. Payments which were being -- which were -- the domestic payments which were happening within the country could not be undertaken because the Social Accounting Office was down. So for all practical purposes, the banking system, the financial system in the way it operated before the start of the war was not functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could direct your attention to page 13 of this statement, page 13. This relates to some text that's found on pages 58 and 59 of your report, looking at paragraph 21 now of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 21. Page 13, paragraph 21, footnote 213.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 213, because I don't see paragraph. I only see pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. You see footnote 213 there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the footnote 213.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What appears under that is the text in your report that is based here, this is based exclusively on your interview with Mr. Backovic. And in your report you say: "These accounts and funds were crucial to ensure financial operations of local communities, both to collect funds from abroad and to purchase goods needed for survival of the population..." et cetera. "Once the formerly occupied territories were set free, economic activity returned and it was necessary to reactivate the financial sector." And then you conclude: "An additional complication was the fact that in some territories, such as Herzegovina, there was not a single bank as a legal entity." Now, are you sure that Mr. Backovic said this to you, because he first of all indicates this is not even clear what you are referring to, and then he says: "This cannot in any way stem from my discussion with Mr. Cvikl." So is it true that you did not discuss with him or that he these statements cannot be attributed to him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were discussing with Mr. Backovic that -- what was the issue of the legal entities. And as you know very well, and we discussed it, and he knows very well, in the area of Herzegovina, there were no legal entities up to the establishment of Mostar ska banka. We were discussing in 1995, 1996 his view which was also then expressed by his actual being member of the board of governments of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually abolishing, annulling the decision by the government of National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 establishing Hrvatska banka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually I think I'm more interested in what I said and when he said it. Do I understand you to be saying that although you may not have discussed this in December 2007 at the Holiday Inn, you discussed this with Mr. Backovic back in 1995, is that the basis of this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No-no. We were discussing the situation in the banking system in -- during the war. As you know, he was in a different bank, right, Komercijalna banka or whatever it was and we were discussing this very issue. And here I'm explaining that this section, this footnote is the section 3.34, so it is the what were the situation at the start of the war. And the situation at the start of the war is that there were no legal entity. And this legal entity --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Cvikl, to cut you off. We understand what your position is. I'm trying to get you to respond to my question which is: What did Mr. Backovic say to you? He says he didn't talk to you about this. I'm trying to ask you whether that's true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be allowed, I think this is one instance where the gentleman is trying to directly answer the question. There are no quotation marks attributed to in the footnote, and so they are talking about a particular issue. I think that's what Mr. Cvikl is trying to now recount, what was the gist of the conversation regarding legal entities. Maybe the gentleman in Sarajevo didn't quite understand or doesn't quite remember, but I think Mr. Cvikl should be given an opportunity in this instance to directly answer the question being posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if he'd directly answer the question being posed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will because -- may I, the Judges?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the paragraph 58 which he discuss has two important sentences in the last section. The first sentence talks, an additional complication was the fact that in some territories such as Herzegovina there were not a single bank as a legal entity at the beginning of the war. There were only local branches of either Sarajevo-based banks, I believe also the banks which he was one of the deputy heads, and there was also a branch of a bank from Slovenia, Ljubljanska banka. So we were talking about while he disputes to the decision of the governor of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Andric of creation Mostarska banka DV because he himself has been against it in year 1994. And you can see that by the decision where the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina annulled the decision, but he was aware of the fact which I'm here stating, that in the beginning not a single bank was a legal entity and thus it was logical to establish a legal entity which I explain later in the text. I'm saying, I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President -- I am sorry, Mr. Cvikl. Mr. President, I don't believe my question is being answered. I think it's being evaded. I am asking the witness whether the statement that Mr. Backovic disavows having spoken about with Mr. Cvikl, whether in fact they discussed --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you discuss this at the Holiday Inn in December 2007 or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: His response on footnote 213 is that he says it's not too clear to me what this refers to, this cannot in any way stem from my discussion with Mr. Cvikl. I'm here explaining what does this refer to. Of course if you would ask Mr. Backovic whether he is agreeing to the decision of establishing Hrvatska banka Mostar DV, and he would be under oath, he would explain this to you very detailed. But of course he avoids responding to this because you should understand, Mr. Prosecutor, that there were disputes between representative of National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina what was actually happening. If I would want to get all the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm going to move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time left, Mr. Registrar? Please move on, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think I have about 30 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer, I also would like to ask Mr. Cvikl really to try to answer and to talk about those points which are asked from you by Mr. Stringer. We have 20 minutes more and you would like to leave tonight, so then let us do that and in a way save us the time and save for you the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, if you turn to page 16 of the Backovic statement. There is -- I'm looking at the text that is linked to your footnote 529. This is text that's based upon an interview of Mr. Backovic and Neven Tomic. And in this text you are saying -- you are talking about the effect of hyperinflation in various areas 1992, 1993. You talk about the Muslim majority area, you talk about the Republika Srpska area, index of retail prices. You go on to say: "Presentation of inflationary movements in the whole of BH has been complicated by the use of multiple or parallel currencies." You continue to go on, you say that: "... in the case of the Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina the Deutschemark was used throughout the country. In this context, hyperinflation Deutschemark terms was never an issue although even prices for goods expressed in Deutschemarks rose many-fold during 1992, 1993 because of shortages caused by supply bottlenecks." Now, you attribute this text to your interviews with Mr. Backovic and Mr. Tomic, but in fact the source of this information comes from one of the books that you brought to the Tribunal; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 19 where I then at the end also have the last sentence have many footnotes, and most of those footnotes relate to the IMF and the recent economic developments report of the World Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the last sentence I'm saying that there were -- that, yes, despite the fact that you have parallel Deutschemark as a currency, there were also inflation increased for goods expressed in Deutschemark. And that's why I say even prices for most goods expressed in Deutschemark rose many points. And we were discussing with Mr. Backovic and Mr. Tomic how kilo of sugar was not 1 Deutschemark, but it was 4 or 6 or 8 Deutschemark because that was due to the short supply of goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've got to listen to my question in the limited time. You told Judge Prandler that you would do that so I'm going to hold you to your promise. Turn to one of your exhibits 1D 02959. 2959. This is the book -- page 26 of the book. It's in sanction. It's on the screen. But I need to go to page 26. Here we go. Can you see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. If we could blow it up. Because it seems to me, sir, that what you've done here is to put in your report virtually the same text or actually just copied the text from the book. You put it into your report and then you indicated that Mr. Backovic and Mr. Tomic were the sources of this information, when, in fact, the information is itself found in the book on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see where -- I'm going to read from part of 2959. "The net effect was the hyperinflation in 1992, 1993." And then there's a reference to footnote 36. It says: "In the Bosniak majority area the index of retail prices rose over 730-fold in 1992, and 440-fold in 1993." That's the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the -- I am sourcing here the IMF report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. But the problem is in your report you don't source the IMF, you report Enver Backovic and Neven Tomic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry, if you look to my report page 123, the paragraph 90 starts: "The net effect was the hyperinflation of 1992, 1993." Then it says: "In the Bosniak majority area, the index of retail prices rose ...", blah, blah, blah, and then it says footnote 526. At footnote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. The first -- the second sentence in the Muslim majority the index of retail prices rose over 730 times in 1992 and 440 times in 1993, and then there's a footnote 526, and footnote 526 is the IMF report. I'm citing Mr. Backovic and Mr. Neven Tomic just on the issue of the so-called raising of goods, and throughout that report I continue: "In the Republika Srpska areas the index of" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, you don't need to read the text to us. We see it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not reading. I'm only would like to explain to the Judges that I am not -- I am quoting Mr. Backovic and Mr. Tomic only on the last sentence of that paragraph. Throughout the paragraph we were explained the hyperinflation. I'm correctly quoting the IMF report. And I would appreciate if you would apologise to me because you have said that I'm quoting Mr. Backovic and Mr. Tomic incorrectly. I'm not quoting them. I'm quoting the IMF and the recent economic developments report of the World Bank, and I've done that correctly. You implied that I haven't done that incorrectly but you misinterpret and you missed the one footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we can agree to disagree on that, sir. I'm pointing out that in fact -- well, we don't need to argue about it, I think both of our positions are out there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In black and white in my report I quote the IMF report, not them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go to the next exhibit, P 00925. P 00925, in binder number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 925. While you are looking for that, I'm going to take you back to this footnote from the World Bank report on inflation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat, 00?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In binder 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we put it up on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have here. P 00925. I don't see it in binder 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, it's in one of the separate folders. Whatever is on the ELMO is not correct. 925.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It is not in binder 1, it is the folder mentioned 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. This is a document that's in evidence in the case. It's a compilation of the value of the Croatian dinar against the German mark at various periods throughout 1992 and 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is a decision to appoint and authorize Jadranko Prlic to represent the government of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then move on, set that aside. I've got the wrong exhibit number, maybe we can sort that out. I'll go ahead to the next thing. Oh, okay. 9255. Let's try that. P 09255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is where?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Binder 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the reason I ask last night to read the documents, but, it was not approved. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does this, in fact, reflect tremendous hyperinflation in respect to the Croatian dinar throughout 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second. This is -- what is the basis of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a compilation from various published reports from the Vijesnik, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we have -- yeah, we have said that in the 1992 there was high inflation in Republic of Croatia up to the reform, which I believe took place sometime in 1994, 1993. And we have seen, as cited in this report, that the high inflation from the -- that high inflation was also present in the war territories, that what, I believe, is important is that high inflation in Herceg-Bosna was to a certain extent lower than the inflation in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina territory. That is what is the essence of the discussion where we have seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to turn you now -- well, first of all, I want to direct your attention or remind you of some testimony you gave on Tuesday of this week. You were asked about schools, schools being opened, universities being opened, and you made a comparison between the situation in Sarajevo and Mostar. And I'm looking at page 35297 of the transcript. Actually, 35296 I'll start. You are staying: "... the value added, the importance of the Defence council was actually in September 1992 when schools were re-opened because of activity of Croatian Defence Council of [HZ HB], not just the elementary schools, but also from the report I could read that the university re-opened its classes, first in Neum, later, again, in Mostar." And then continuing, I'm going to skip down on page 35297, you say: "I understood from discussion with my, you know, counterpart that actually I don't know how much of, you know, really, elementary schools and how -- whether the university operated in Sarajevo. I don't think it did. But university of Mostar did operate and students went to these classes in Neum, and later, you know, they stayed home." First of all, do you know -- do you know yourself for sure the extent or when the elementary schools opened, held classes in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this something the Judges should rely on your testimony for to the extent you are implying that they weren't open in relation to the Herceg-Bosna schools?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm going to object. He never stated that they were not operating in Sarajevo. He said he didn't know to what extent. So let's put the testimony in context. The added value is that if schools are open, folks will stay in the area and won't go outside to other countries. That was the gist of the discussion. But he never indicated or said that he knew for a fact and he didn't state for a fact that the schools in Sarajevo were not operating. He said he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if that -- and we can try to confirm that that indeed is his testimony, I can move on. It appeared to us that a different suggestion was being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, Sarajevo schools?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that I didn't know the extent, and the reason -- if you allow me, the reason why I have said this is because when we were meeting officials from Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then I visited some of the officials at their home, I could see in their home kids being taught at home because in a particular area of Sarajevo because of the snipers, they could not go to the part where the schools were there. But I have said last Tuesday that I didn't know how and when they actually opened, but I know for a fact on the basis of the information provided and the budget expenditures that schools were much more operational in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and they would not be operational if that would be only responsibility of the local communities. That is all what am I saying. The valued added of the region-wide territory, or the region-wide authorities to re-open schools was presented to me with facts on the documents and I appreciate those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to turn, please, to Exhibit P 00714, which is in binder number 1. 00714.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a decree on the establishment and work of the University of Mostar during war or imminent threat of war dated the 6th of November, 1992. It appears over the signature of Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I might have seen it. I saw a couple of these decisions establishing the hospitals, university, schools, but I don't recall all the details. But I have assumed that such a document was there because otherwise it would not be -- without this document it would not be possible to undertake government expenditures to an institution which does not exist, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, I just asked you if you had seen it before. That's all. That's all. Article 2, please. The decree provides that "the name of the university shall be as follows," so they are naming it Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, University of Mostar. Item 4 in Article 2 provides that the language used at the university shall be Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It continues: "The university shall take over all moveable and immovable property in addition to the rights and obligations of the former Dzemal Bijedic university" --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bijedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Bijedic. "... Bijedic university and its members." Right? And then going to the very end, Article 34, says that, "on the day this decree enters into force, the activity of all organs of the Dzemal Bijedic university in Mostar and its members shall cease." Now, Mr. Cvikl, in order to fill the void, if you will, caused by the war and the collapse of the social institutions, what is the economic benefit of mandating that a particular language must be used at a public academic institution? Is there any such economic benefit from this sort of requirement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you are aware, but before the war we were taught Serbo-Croatian, and so here the -- it would be, you know, the language used at the university could be either Serbian or Croatian, and since Serbian were aggressors and at that time there was the Croatian language or the -- it's for me logical that the language is Croatian. It could be Serbian, but, I guess, Serbian were at that time, of course, the language of an aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is there an economic benefit from requiring that a specific language be used?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is appropriate that the university in a country which is named Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and with this country I believe at this point had only two official languages and that were named as the Serbo-Croatian language, Serbian or Croatian, it is logical that this entity Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina defined which is the language thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I think you've answered my question. I've got another question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Economic benefit is there because it could -- here it could say it should be English, but then it of course would be quite costly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll ask you the next question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I think you have three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm doing my best under these circumstance, Mr. President, to reach the end of my outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the intentions and the efforts the HVO were to simply fill a void, is it necessary to rename the institution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm -- I think it's beyond the scope of the gentleman's purpose for being here which was -- presented an economic report. Obviously he may be able to answer the question, but he is here as an economist having looked at economic measures that were taken. I understand what Mr. Stringer is trying to do, but I do think this is well beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, but education is mentioned on several occasions in the report, you know, so he must have looked into the issue of education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: For me the question is focused on economy. The question is, does it give an economic benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Shall I say it again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They renamed the university. If they are simply filling in the void and trying to keep things going in the absence of a central government, it's not necessary to change the name of the university; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for the following reason: I have said before that it is, for me, quite logical that they have said which are the language. They have two options, being Croatian being Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm asking you now the next question which is the name of the institution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will respond to this. I will respond to this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I intend to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Answer my question, please, about the change of the name, whether, in your view, it's necessary to fill the void?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This became a new legal entity. In order to be a new legal entity, you have to establish it as a legal entity because otherwise it cannot be financed from the budget. If you want to give money to a budget user, you have to define as a legal entity. If it would not be re-established, then the funds shall be provided by the central government. In that very case, the teachers, the pupils, the students, they would go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've just got a couple more questions. I'm going to ask for the Trial Chamber's indulgence, I think in respect of this particular witness it's not too much to ask for an extra five minutes, and that's all I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try to wrap it up in two or three minutes, because if you now want to ask questions, I couldn't see any relevance in it, but I don't know what you are planning to do. So please do endeavour to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I will do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a different subject on customs and border crossings. First of all -- we are finished with that. In your earlier testimony you indicated that you had not seen establishment of the customs crossing points by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I believe, not all the way up to 1995. This is page 35275 of your testimony. You were asked: "Did you come across any legislation signed by the president of the presidency Alija Izetbegovic at the time when Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared independent whereby they established border crossings in a customs administration?" You said: "No, I have not." Is it possible, sir, that you have missed that, or have you comprehensively reviewed all the legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have said in my testimony that even in 1995 when we came into Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no customs clerks with the head Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina customs office. That only was established after IFOR entered and after long deliberation of Bosnia-Herzegovina customs clerks were first put in place, and then later on, I believe, the joint customs office of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm asking you a different -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the customs officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm asking you a different question. From your testimony you were asked, "did you come across any legislation signed by the president of the presidency Alija Izetbegovic?" You said, "no, I have not." So that is my question. Isn't it true, sir, that there was, in fact, customs and border crossing legislation signed by President Izetbegovic at the beginning of independence and thereafter in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said, and I repeat, the country was internationally recognized, it adopted a lot of laws, but it was not an effective state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you -- sorry to interrupt. You must answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You are saying -- I'm asking you, did you see legislation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not reviewed all the legislation. I have reviewed the legislation which I was asked to do. And I was not doing analysis of what was happening at all activities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was looking into the analysis of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, the answer is no, full stop, please. You are really abusing of time and this is wasting time. And that's not what you are supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, it's no. Full stop. Mr. Stringer. No, will you please shut up now and only answer questions. Please. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If -- well, I'll try to facilitate this. If you can turn to the last two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can shut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The last two exhibits. P 10768. 10768. Which is in a separate small attachment, and also 10770. 10768. I see you -- okay. 10768. "Decree law on customs law." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dated the 11th of April 1992, very lengthy document. So is it true, sir, that you were not aware of this at the time you told the Trial Chamber on Tuesday that you had not seen any or you indicated that you were not aware of any legislation signed by president Izetbegovic on customs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen and I have not made analysis of all the legislation that was issued at that time, but I'm confirming in 1995, when we were there, there were nobody from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a customs clerks on the customs points as we were entering into the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that it was -- it was a country, it issued laws, it did not put laws into place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much, Mr. Witness, thank you for testifying here. Mr. Usher, please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have a choice: Either we have a short break because I have an oral decision that will take 3 or 4 minutes, and I know that the Petkovic Defence needs 5 minutes. So what shall we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, not even 5 minutes. We really will be about one minute, I think, if that helps. Yes, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute. Well, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We need to go into private session for it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I also have at least a couple of minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how many more minutes are there on the tape? [In English] 10 minutes? 10 minutes. [Interpretation] Well, we have about 10 minutes. I think it's best to use the 10 minutes we have and then to just adjourn rather than break now and start again. Let us moving straight away into private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's terribly simple, although an ex parte motion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel, I need to indicate on record that we are now in private session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is important because it has to do with next week, and we should issue this oral decision following the motion by the Stojic Defence filed on the 14th of January, 2009 for addition of three documents to the 65 ter list. The Trial Chamber was seized of a motion, a partly confidential motion filed by the Stojic Defence in which it is requested that three documents be added to the 65 ter list. The documents are annexed or attached to enclosures A, B, and C, of the motion. By this decision, the Trial Chamber is going to rule only on the merits in the motion for request to add annex A to the 65 ter list of the Stojic Defence. The A annex includes an expert before by Davor Marijan entitled "On the World Connection of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina" that contains 39 pages. And the Stojic Defence first argues that if the Trial Chamber were to grant the motion, it will submit the expert report during the testimony of the expert witness scheduled next week starting on the 19th of January, 2009. In support of its motion, the Stojic Defence says that this is a probative report directly connected to the case by the Stojic Defence. It was admitted in the Naletilic and Martinovic case in which Davor Marijan was an expert witness in September 2002. It further argues that the need for this report appeared only recently. The Trial Chamber following deliberations rules that the part of the motion regarding annex A should be dismissed on the following grounds: Firstly, that this time-period of four days between disclosure of annex A, a very bulky document at that, and the testimony of the witness is too short a period, far too short a period, and does not allow the other parties in the trial to have enough time to prepare for their respective cross-examination on that document and the topic contained therein. The Trial Chamber further notes that this time-period is so short that it does not even allow the other parties to the proceedings to file a response to the motion in the time-period scheduled for it or in a reasonable period of time. Secondly, the Trial Chamber is of the view that the ground set forth by the Stojic Defence for annex A not to be found in the 65 ter list is groundless. Indeed, it is not enough to tell the Trial Chamber that the need to add evidence to the 65 ter list appeared lately. The requesting party also has to demonstrate the objective grounds on account of which it could not materially have included the document in their 65 ter list when it was filed. For instance, the fact that the Defence did not have the document when it filed the list, in spite of due diligence, and the Stojic Defence presented no objective reasons. On the contrary, the circumstance that as the report of annex A was filed in the Naletilic case back in September 2002, over five years ago in other words, shows that the Stojic Defence could have known of the document and could have apprised itself of the document well before it filed its 65 ter list. Thirdly, the Trial Chamber notes that the Stojic Defence presents this report as being an expert report and that the Stojic Defence knows, of course, that expert reports have to be filed well ahead of time to the other parties to the proceedings meeting the requirements of Rule 92 bis. As such -- 94 bis. If it presented this report four days before the witness begins to testify, that is twisting the provisions of Rule 94 bis. The Trial Chamber deems that disclosing at this stage such a late disclosure of the document in spite or against all the rules of the guide-lines by the Trial Chamber and against the rules of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence is really indeed abusing the rules. This is the very reason why the Trial Chamber is of the view that it was not necessary to wait for responses by the other parties to dismiss this part. Regarding annexes B and C, the Stojic Defence specifies that if the Trial Chamber were to grant its request for the two annexes, they will be presented when Slobodan Bocic [phoen] testifies, his testimony being schedule as of the 26th of January 2009. Therefore, the Trial Chamber orders the parties to file their respective replies on that parts of the Stojic motion, the annexes B and C, by Monday 19th of January, 2009. You may proceed Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. That was our very last witness. I believe we have 13 minutes left on the clock, so -- despite our best efforts, we cut it very close. My request deals with the following witness who is about to appear Marijan Davor. As I understand he has a report, we've seen it, but at this point in time in keeping with a previous ruling from another case, in the Gotovina case, we are requesting that Mr. Davor Marijan provide to us and disclose any drafts to that particular report that he may have prepared. On 17 November, 2008, in the Gotovina case, the Defence requested from a Prosecution expert that they -- that the Prosecution disclose the draft expert reports. The Prosecution responded, they objected at the time. It was discussed and on 3rd December, 2008, as I understand it, Judge Orie, while he did not vehemently issue an order that there should be such a disclosure, he did indicate -- he allowed it up to the expert himself who obviously agreed in that instance. So I don't want to overstate what the Trial Chamber did in that instance. But in this case, we do believe that the drafts would be important in assisting us for our cross-examination. I make this request particularly since, as you may recall, Your Honours, I did request for 90 minutes to cross-examine the gentleman. My request was denied. This was made back in December. With less time, more preparation is needed, and so it looks like I will have 30 or 20 minutes, so with that in mind, I'm making this request that he be ordered to produce all drafts that were presented to the Defence prior to finalising the report that we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, is that a problem? Could you possibly disclose to Mr. Karnavas and the other parties the report in the Gotovina case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not the Gotovina, we want drafts of Mr. Davor Marijan's reports, all his drafts, that's what we want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all these drafts and the preparatory takes. Because you mentioned Gotovina, so I didn't understand, I thought he was a witness in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, in the Gotovina case, the issue came up. And it's another Trial Chamber who addressed this issue. And as I've indicated, Judge Orie did not make a firm ruling and left it up to the expert himself, I don't want to speculate what Judge Orie would have done had he been pressed. But in keeping with that, I'm making this particular request because we do view this gentleman as a hostile witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really cannot respond to this request from my learned colleague. I don't know whether Mr. Marijan has any thesis and notes at all and without him I'm unable to answer that. We did have a meeting. Now, whether he has these drafts or notes or whatever, I really can't say and can't speak for him. But I do feel a professional duty, Your Honour, and it is this: Just to respond briefly and give the reasons with respect to your ruling a moment ago. The Stojic Defence felt that we should not use the findings but that we should present them to the Court precisely because the question might be raised as to whether he provided findings in other trials and whether these are contradictory findings, and that is why we wanted - and regardless of the fact that you refused our request - but with your permission if you allow us we would like to attach the findings in our binder that go with the report of expert witness Marijan. So we weren't going to use it in the first place, we just wanted to attach it. We didn't wish to examine on it. But for all -- the benefit of all parties, we just wanted to show what the findings dealt with and to show that they weren't contrary to the findings that we are going to present before this Trial Chamber. So I felt it my duty to tell you that. We didn't do it out of disrespect for the Trial Chamber but quite the opposite, to make the Court's job easier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Efforts to make our lives easier, thank you very much for that. Well, could you call your expert, Mr. Davor Marijan and ask him whether he has the document requested by Mr. Karnavas? If he says yes, I can give them to you, he can fax them to you, and you can then disclose them to the Prosecution and Mr. Karnavas. I don't know. I don't know where documents are, maybe there aren't any, but you could put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't do that because I don't understand what it's about. So I can't do that. Perhaps if I read the transcript again, I will understand it better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you inform Ms. Nozica what you are expecting because you can always discuss in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I want to be on the record on this one and I want to be very clear and to the extent that I wasn't clear, I apologise. As I understand it, the gentleman has been working at this report over the course of a year or two years. If he has prepared drafts which he has shared with the Defence or with Mr. Stojic and then eventually he comes up with a final draft, as it was requested in the Gotovina case, I am requesting that all prior drafts be provided to us to see if there was some sort of evolutionary change at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the drafts, so if he's -- produces a first draft report and a second draft. Well, my colleague would like the Prosecution to come in in the cross-examination, but of course I'd ruled on the matter because I said that if it exists it might also be disclosed to the Prosecution, and Mr. Stringer will indicate whether that if it exists that he'd like to have it too. Mr. Stringer. We've run out of tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we don't take a position on this request of the Prlic Defence, Mr. President. If the Trial Chamber ultimately decides that something has to be disclosed, we'd like a copy also. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you and so we meet again next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
